validator_run.raw_output: raw exit 0 on the integrated SHA; go test ./... = 0 with 35 packages

review_notes.measured_on_the_user_repository: Fifteen error findings before, none of the sampled ones true. After: the same repository reports six, five of which are genuine innerHTML writes in dashboard templates.
review_notes.root_cause: The hardcoded-secret value class was [0-9\\-], so a hyphen stood in for the required digit and every hyphenated placeholder read as random. The sql-injection rule's .* let the scan skip a safe + and match a later one.
review_notes.round_1: REJECT. Removing the hyphen broke real secrets whose digits cluster at one edge: AURUM-FAKE-CANARY-VALUE-7777, a fixture of tests/unit/AUR-442.go, stopped matching and AUR-442's acceptance went from 0 to 1. The reviewer isolated the regex in a plain Go program to prove it, outside any script of the candidate's.
review_notes.round_2: REJECT, and the fault was the coordinator's: read_paths lacked the CLI's build closure, so the card's own accept could not pass regardless of the regex -- exit 79 on missing-input:internal/prompt. Fixed with go list -deps.
review_notes.round_3: APPROVE. Sealed run 0, and the reviewer confirmed no product code changed since the SHA they had already audited.
review_notes.measured_limitation: The reviewer took the gap the builder had called theoretical and measured it exhaustively: values of 6 to 8 characters escape when the digit/letter split lands near 4/4 with no padding -- token = \"9000User\" is the concrete case -- and from 9 characters on no split escapes. Every real secret in the 16 to 64 character range this rule targets satisfies some branch.
review_notes.declared_costs: A credential with no digit at all is missed. The reviewer looked for a common digit-free format and found none: a real AWS key is digit-free with probability around 0.16%, and hex-with-only-letters is not a generator output. A diceware passphrase is the one plausible case, and it is declared.
